reviewScope: Three genuine native synchronization exercises and fifteen actual language bodies.

questions.algorithm: Acquire both adjacent fork locks in increasing physical-index order, eat once, then release both, for each requested bite.
questions.review: Read primary QuestionA/QuestionB Philosopher/Chopstick classes and all five actual independent bodies. The explicitly stated blocking-fork variant completes every requested bite, unlike a try-lock attempt loop that may give up. Each worker orders its two distinct physical fork indices, including wraparound, holds both through the real Eat callback and drops both before the next iteration/return. Native semaphore/condition-variable/Atomics ownership observations reject eating without locks, releasing another worker fork, leaked locks and incomplete meals. No canonical eating order is forced: the oracle checks exact role multiplicities and the private observer checks exclusive fork ownership. All 47 fixtures cover n=2..6, zero/four bites, launch permutations and entry delays. A source-neutral initial acquisition schedule waits until each worker has either obtained its first fork or is blocked on an already held first fork, allowing increasing and decreasing acyclic lock orders while exposing the all-left-first circular wait deterministically. The phase never forces a philosopher to acquire a currently unavailable fork before others progress. Twenty compiled programs reject no-lock, leaked-lock and circular-wait bodies while accepting descending global acquisition. Native callback completion and final release are observed; the no-cycle correctness argument supplies the scheduler-independent reasoning that finite executions alone cannot establish.

questions.algorithm: Wait on the predecessor semaphore, perform private worker work, then signal the successor semaphore.
questions.review: Read primary Foo and startup example and all five independent bodies. Each calls owned Work once; role 0 never waits, role 1 waits gate 0 and signals gate 1 after Work return, role 2 waits gate 1. Native managed/Java/std/Python threads and Node worker_threads actually execute, with readiness barriers, launch permutations and delayed entries. Private Work rejects overlap with predecessor work and duplicate calls; work completion is not synthesized from a sorted answer. Initially empty counting permits handle both signal-before-wait and wait-before-signal schedules. A lost-wakeup risk in the JavaScript parent observation loop was corrected by passing its single observed counter value into Atomics.wait. All 24 launch/delay fixtures run in every language; fifteen compiled native-worker programs reject no-wait/wrong-gate bodies and accept valid surplus signals, proving the observer does not demand an exact reference API call trace. Context ownership, finite API-call caps, independent case gates and blocking rather than busy polling are reviewed. Bounded observed runs complement the handoff correctness proof; they do not claim proof of every scheduler or arbitrary realtime fairness.

questions.algorithm: One permit baton handed to the unique owner of each next integer after its role-bound Print callback finishes.
questions.review: Read primary QuestionB/FizzBuzzThread/NumberThread and all five actual bodies. Four native threads/workers execute each case; public sequential QuestionA is not substituted. Each role scans values increasingly, handles divisibility by 15 before 3/5, consumes its own gate before printing and signals the next owner only after Print returns. Same-role consecutive integers preserve a permit for the next wait; limit 0 invokes no print. Context callback checks correct worker role, exact next number, nonoverlap and completion rather than trusting a returned token list. Managed/Java/Python gates are native semaphores; C++ mutex/condition-variable permits and JS SharedArrayBuffer/Atomics provide actual cross-thread handoffs. All 51 fixtures include every four-worker launch permutation, all entry-delay masks, limit 0/1/3/5/15/16/30/100 and repeated independent contexts. Twenty compiled variants reject missing waits, incorrect role at multiples of 15 and wrong successor handoff, while accepting strided per-role scans. The supplied bounds/count caps and snapshot-free scalar algorithm costs match the actual implementations. Finite observed schedules complement, rather than replace, the semaphore induction proof.

languageBindingReview.csharp: RunOrdered borrows abstract SyncContext and synchronously hands off permits around Work. Actual managed Thread callbacks receive per-worker wrappers sharing native SemaphoreSlim gates; private completion state is locked. Background threads and bounded waits prevent a deadlock mutant from retaining the test process indefinitely. Concurrent FizzBuzz uses its distinct FizzContext API with four real workers and one permit baton. The owner predicate checks multiples of 15 first; the private role-bound printer rejects duplicate, overlapping or out-of-order work, and no user-created output array is accepted. Dining Philosophers uses its own ForkContext API, real exclusive fork permits, owned worker identity and per-role meal counts. Global physical-index acquisition handles the wraparound role; callback return precedes dropping locks. The controlled initial acquisition phase admits both ascending and descending deadlock-free orders.
